extracted_notes.text: Canada is influenced by British, French and Indigenous cultures and traditions.
Canadian identity shifted from primarily British-based to multicultural between the 1960s and 1970s.
As a whole, Canada is in theory a cultural mosaic of regional ethnic subcultures with diverse areas and ethnic enclaves.
The use of the maple leaf as a symbol dates to the early 18th century in New France. The maple leaf is depicted on Canada's current and previous flags and on the arms of Canada.

Canada's official tartan, known as the "maple leaf tartan", reflects the colours of the maple leaf through the seasons--green in the spring, gold in the early autumn, red at the first frost, and brown after falling.
The arms of Canada are closely modelled after those of the United Kingdom, with French and distinctive Canadian elements replacing or added to those derived from the British version.

Other prominent symbols include the national motto, "A mari usque ad mare" ("from sea to sea"), the sports of ice hockey and lacrosse, the beaver, Canada goose, common loon, Canadian horse, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Canadian Rockies, and, more recently, the Indigenous totem pole and Inuksuk.

Canadian cuisine items such as Canadian beer, maple syrup, Nanaimo bars, butter tarts, and the Quebec dishes of poutine and tourtiere, alongside material items such as tuques, canoes and Hudson's Bay point blanket are considered as uniquely Canadian.

Canadian coins feature many of these symbols: the loon on the $1 coin, the coat of arms on the 50C/ piece, and the beaver on the nickel. An image of the monarch appears on $20 bank notes and the obverse of coins.
Canada's official national sports are ice hockey and lacrosse.

accordion_data.title: Maple Leaf Tartan Colors
accordion_data.intro_text: Canada's official tartan reflects the changing colors of the maple leaf throughout the different seasons.

blocks.text_content: While the maple leaf is central, Canada employs a wide array of other symbols to represent its geography, wildlife, and heritage.

The **arms of Canada** are closely modeled after the United Kingdom's, but they incorporate French and uniquely Canadian elements. These are joined by a national motto, *"A mari usque ad mare"* (**from sea to sea**), and symbols of the natural world.
